nodes.label: Irrigated Bronze Age states
nodes.full: The Bronze Age states of Mesopotamia, the Indus and Egypt, linked by long-distance trade, are the setting that moves oil crops and fats between regions (Bedigian 2011 ch.1 p.3).

nodes.label: Climate sets the fat
nodes.full: Animal fat in the cool north, plant oil in the warm south and east: the environment decides which fat a region will use for thousands of years.

nodes.label: Rendering
nodes.full: The first way humans extracted fat from animals: heating the tissue until the fat separates.

nodes.label: First butter
nodes.full: Neolithic herders milking sheep and goats make butter, the first dairy fat.

nodes.label: Clarified butter
nodes.full: In hot Mesopotamia butter is clarified so it will keep — the ancestor of ghee.

nodes.label: Olive domesticated
nodes.full: Chalcolithic Levant: olive stones and wood show the tree under cultivation.

nodes.label: Olive presses
nodes.full: Late Bronze Age Cyprus and Crete press olives at scale.

nodes.label: Canaanite oil to Egypt
nodes.full: Levantine oil imported to Egypt; olive stones at Uluburun.

nodes.label: Ebla’s inspectors
nodes.full: Fraud checks on growers and millers at Ebla.

nodes.label: Palace oil stores
nodes.full: Oil kept in the royal cellars of Ebla, Mari, Ugarit and Minoan Crete.

nodes.label: Crete’s oil export
nodes.full: Crete grows rich on exporting olive oil at the end of the Bronze Age.

nodes.label: Harappan sesame
nodes.full: Sesame is grown in the Indus valley by 2600–2000 BC.

nodes.label: Sesame to Mesopotamia
nodes.full: Sesame and its names move from the Indus to Mesopotamia by 2000 BC.

nodes.label: The oil-plant
nodes.full: Cuneiform texts from 2400 BC name an oil plant, argued to be sesame.

nodes.label: Sesame in Egypt
nodes.full: Sesame seeds among Tutankhamun’s grave goods.

nodes.label: Yale tablets
nodes.full: The oldest recipes put fat in every pot.

nodes.label: Palm fat at Abydos
nodes.full: A tomb fat of about 3000 BC identified as palm oil.

nodes.label: Saharan dairy fat
nodes.full: Milk fat in pots at Takarkori, fifth millennium BC.

nodes.label: Oil-palm shells
nodes.full: Palm endocarps at African sites from about 3000 BC.

nodes.label: The sunflower
nodes.full: Domesticated in eastern North America before 1500 BC.

nodes.label: The soybean
nodes.full: Domesticated in north-east China, 2700 or 1000 BC.

nodes.label: Peruvian peanuts
nodes.full: Peanuts grown in Peru by 2000 BC.

nodes.label: Egypt’s nhh
nodes.full: The identity of the pharaohs’ best oil.

nodes.label: Baltic marine fat in pots
nodes.full: Marine and freshwater foods still cooked as farming arrives.

nodes.label: Blubber lamps
nodes.full: Late Mesolithic lamps of the Ertebølle north.

nodes.label: Neolithic beeswax
nodes.full: Beeswax in early Turkish pots from about 7000 BC.

nodes.label: Indus pot lipids
nodes.full: Mostly animal fat in Harappan pots; little dairy.

nodes.label: The Indus cow
nodes.full: Fuller on the assumption that cattle meant milk.

nodes.label: Secondary products
nodes.full: Sherratt on when people began to milk.

nodes.label: Near Oceania tree crops
nodes.full: Almond, coconut and candlenut at New Guinea sites.

nodes.label: Egypt’s butter fat
nodes.full: Butter fat, ox fat and goose fat in Egyptian records; cheese at Saqqara.

nodes.label: Egypt’s ben, balanos and castor
nodes.full: Oils Egypt grew: moringa, balanites, castor, lettuce.

nodes.label: The olive in Egypt
nodes.full: A sacred tree at Heliopolis, oil imported from Syria.

nodes.label: China’s pigs and dogs
nodes.full: Meat and fat from pigs and dogs from Yangshao to Shang; no milk.

nodes.label: Chekiang sesame and peanuts
nodes.full: Third-millennium seeds that most scholars reject.

nodes.label: El Gigante avocados
nodes.full: A tree managed for larger, thicker-skinned fruit from about 5600 BC.

nodes.label: Banpo brassica seeds
nodes.full: Brassica seeds in an early Neolithic village; possibly for oil.

edges: Herding regions supply animal fat and dairy, as Kiple’s environmental account of fat consumption explains.
Rendered sheep fat is the cooking fat of the Babylonian recipes.
Butter’s Mesopotamian form is clarified, which is what lets it keep in a hot climate.
The domesticated olive is what the Late Bronze Age presses of Cyprus and Crete process.
Zohary and Mueller both place Cretan and Levantine oil on the sea routes to Egypt.
Mueller ties the Ebla inspectors to the same palace oil economy.
Mueller’s palace oil stores and Kiple’s Cretan export are two accounts of the same Bronze Age oil economy.
Large-scale processing and Crete’s oil export belong to the same Late Bronze Age olive economy, though the two sources are independent.
Bedigian and Fuller date sesame to the Indus before it reaches Mesopotamia by 2000 BC.
The Mesopotamian oil-plant texts of about 2400 BC are the written trace of the imported crop, as Bedigian reads them.
Sesame’s spread westward continues to Egypt by about 1500 BC.
The long-distance trade of the Bronze Age states carried sesame and its names between the Indus and Mesopotamia.
Peanut in Peru and sunflower in eastern North America are the New World’s two earliest oil crops in this folio.
The sunflower and the soybean, two of today’s great oils, were domesticated on different continents with no contact.
Dairy fat in the Sahara and palm fat in an Egyptian tomb are Africa’s two oldest fat records in this folio.
The palm-oil jar at Abydos and the palm shells of West and Central Africa are the same story seen from the Egyptian and the African end.
Akkadian šamaššammū and Egyptian nhh are two oil names whose identity scholars cannot settle.
Cooking pots and lamps of the same Baltic hunter-gatherers both ran on marine and freshwater fat.
The north’s fish and sea-mammal fat is the other side of the climate baseline that sets animal fat in the cool north.
Beeswax and butter are the two Neolithic lipids found in the pots of the earliest farmers.
The Harappan sesame crop and the fat in Harappan pots are two parts of the same food economy.
Fuller’s caution about assuming milk is the context for the Indus lipid result, which finds little dairy.
Sherratt’s milking argument and the first butter are the two ends of the same question, when herds began to give fat.
Coconut and almond in New Guinea and oil-palm fat in an Egyptian tomb are two tropical tree-fat records of the folio.
Lucas rejects the palm-oil reading of Abydos and finds mainly animal fats in Egyptian tombs.
Egypt’s butter fat and Mesopotamia’s clarified butter are the same hot-country fat.
Lucas’s list of Egyptian oils is the setting for the argument over nhh.
Lucas’s Syrian oil and Reisner’s Fourth Dynasty imports are the Egyptian side of the Canaanite oil trade.
China’s pig fat and the Near East’s first butter are two ways the world’s early farmers got animal fat, one without milk and one with it.
Both entries concern a South American peanut turning up where it should not be, in Peru’s case in the right place and in Chekiang’s the wrong one.
The Honduran avocado and the Peruvian peanut are the New World’s fat from trees and from a groundnut, in the absence of dairy herds.
Banpo’s brassica seeds and Yangshao’s pigs are the two kinds of fat that early northern China could have drawn on, plant oil and animal fat.
